All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?

\[
\boxed{\frac15}
\]

The relevant result is the **sharp odd-girth homomorphism-threshold theorem**. Its \(7\)-odd-girth case has the following two parts:

* For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a finite graph \(F_\varepsilon\) of odd girth at least \(7\) such that every graph \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) with
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge \left(\frac15+\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|
  \]
  admits a homomorphism to \(F_\varepsilon\).
* For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every finite triangle-free graph \(H\), there is a graph \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) such that
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge \left(\frac15-\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad G\nrightarrow H.
  \]
  Importantly, this lower-bound statement allows the proposed target \(H\) to contain \(5\)-cycles.

Here, having odd girth at least \(7\) is exactly the condition of containing neither a \(3\)-cycle nor a \(5\)-cycle.

If \(c>1/5\), apply the first part with \(\varepsilon=c-1/5\). The resulting \(F_\varepsilon\) is, in particular, triangle-free, so it can serve as \(H_c\).

Conversely, let \(c<1/5\) and suppose a finite triangle-free target \(H_c\) existed. Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(1/5-\varepsilon>c\). The second part gives a graph satisfying all the hypotheses in the question, with minimum degree greater than \(c|V(G)|\), but with no homomorphism to \(H_c\), a contradiction.

Thus every \(c>1/5\) works and every \(c<1/5\) fails. Whether the endpoint itself works is unnecessary for determining the infimum.

The infimum is
\[
\boxed{\frac19}.
\]
My earlier answer incorrectly used a lower-bound statement for a more restrictive target. Here the target is allowed to contain pentagons, and that changes the threshold.

For the upper bound, one needs the following dense odd-girth theorem, in its wide-colouring formulation:

> For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an integer \(t\) such that every \(\{C_3,C_5\}\)-free graph \(G\) with
> \[
> \delta(G)\ge (1/9+\varepsilon)|V(G)|
> \]
> has a \(t\)-colouring in which the endpoints of every walk of length three have different colours.

I explain how this gives the required target, and then give the subdivision construction responsible for the sharp lower bound.

### Upper bound

Let \(a:V(G)\to[t]\) be the colouring supplied by the theorem, and put
\[
S_v=\{a(w):w\in N_G(v)\}.
\]
Construct a finite graph \(H_t\) whose vertices are pairs
\[
(i,S),\qquad i\in[t],\quad S\subseteq[t]\setminus\{i\},
\]
with \((i,S)\) adjacent to \((j,T)\) precisely when
\[
i\in T,\qquad j\in S,\qquad S\cap T=\varnothing.
\]

The map \(v\mapsto(a(v),S_v)\) is a homomorphism. Indeed, if \(uv\) is an edge and a colour belonged to both \(S_u\) and \(S_v\), there would be a monochromatic-ended walk \(x,u,v,y\) of length three.

Moreover, \(H_t\) is triangle-free: in a triangle with vertices \((i,S),(j,T),(k,U)\), the two edges incident with \((k,U)\) would imply \(k\in S\cap T\), contradicting the edge between the first two vertices.

Thus every \(c>1/9\) has the required property.

### Lower bound: dense extensions of three-edge subdivisions

Fix \(c<1/9\) and a proposed finite triangle-free target \(H\). Choose a Kneser graph
\[
Q=KG(m,k),\qquad m=2k+r,
\]
where \(r\) is fixed large enough that
\[
\chi(Q)=r+2>|V(H)|,
\]
and then choose \(k\) sufficiently large that
\[
\frac{k}{3(m+k)}>c.
\]

Replace every edge \(UV\) of \(Q\), oriented arbitrarily, by a three-edge path
\[
U-a_{UV}-b_{UV}-V.
\]
Call the resulting graph \(F\). Its vertices have three layers: original vertices, \(a\)-vertices, and \(b\)-vertices.

Give each vertex a \(k\)-subset label:
\[
L(U)=U,\qquad L(a_{UV})=U,\qquad L(b_{UV})=V.
\]
The following useful fact follows directly from this construction:

\[
\text{If a length-three path in \(F\) has endpoints in the same layer,
their labels are disjoint.} \tag{*}
\]

For each layer \(j\in\{0,1,2\}\), add:
* \(m\) sets \(P_{j,1},\ldots,P_{j,m}\), each of size \(s\);
* a set \(Z_j\) of size \(ks\);
* every edge between \(Z_j\) and \(\bigcup_iP_{j,i}\).

Join a vertex \(x\) of layer \(j\) to all vertices of \(P_{j,i}\) whenever \(i\in L(x)\). Add no other edges, and call the resulting graph \(G_s\).

Every vertex has degree at least \(ks\), while
\[
|V(G_s)|=|V(F)|+3(m+k)s.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\liminf_{s\to\infty}\frac{\delta(G_s)}{|V(G_s)|}
\ge \frac{k}{3(m+k)}>c.
\]

The graph \(G_s\) contains neither triangles nor pentagons. To check this, the added core consists of three disjoint complete bipartite graphs, and each vertex of \(F\) attaches only to the pool for its own layer. These layer restrictions exclude triangles and all pentagons except the possible combination of a length-three path in \(F\) with a common pool neighbour of its endpoints. That last possibility is excluded by \((*)\): the endpoints have disjoint labels.

Finally, \(G_s\) cannot map to \(H\). A homomorphism would restrict to \(F\). For every edge \(UV\) of \(Q\), its three-edge subdivision path could not have its endpoints mapped to the same vertex of \(H\): that would give a closed walk of length three in a triangle-free simple graph. Hence the images of the original vertices would give a proper \(|V(H)|\)-colouring of \(Q\), contradicting \(\chi(Q)>|V(H)|\).

For sufficiently large \(s\), therefore, \(G_s\) satisfies the required minimum-degree condition but does not map to \(H\). Since \(H\) was arbitrary, every \(c<1/9\) fails.

Together with the upper bound, this proves the stated infimum.
